summary:
AresNav is an interactive Mars exploration and route planning prototype developed by NeuroMars. It combines a 3D Mars globe with public NASA/JPL and USGS map data, historical Curiosity and Perseverance records, science layers, and example mission scenarios. Users can explore the surface, select route endpoints, and test an experimental planner that weighs sampled elevation, slope, geology, thermal map transitions, and known hazards to find a lower-cost path.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex planetary data easier to explore and apply to mission planning. By bringing multiple data sources into one visual tool, AresNav helps users investigate how terrain and scientific context may affect travel across Mars. It is important as an educational demonstration of data-informed planetary exploration and a starting point for future research into intelligent navigation. All routes and mission estimates are experimental and are not certified for operational use.
details:
AresNav — Project Details

Interactive Mars Exploration and Experimental Science-Aware Route Planning

What does our project do and how does it work?

AresNav is an interactive Mars exploration platform that brings map imagery, scientific context, historical rover records, and route planning into one 3D environment.

Built with JavaScript, Node.js, Express, and CesiumJS, AresNav displays Mars as a navigable globe. Users can explore example mission sites at Jezero Crater and Mount Sharp, inspect map features, turn science layers on and off, and view historical Curiosity and Perseverance traverses and stops.

The project also includes an experimental terrain-aware route planner. Users choose a starting point and destination from saved locations or directly on the map. The planner samples NASA Mars Trek MOLA/HRSC elevation data, then considers slope, local elevation variation, mapped USGS geology, MGS TES thermal-map transitions, and known hazards. It uses Theta* pathfinding to search for a lower-cost route across the sampled terrain grid. Results include the route, terrain summaries, confidence notes, and an option to download a text briefing.

AresNav also offers modeled mission estimates, a visual route simulation, coordinate-based elevation lookup, science candidate and exploration-zone information, and a guided tour of the app.

What benefits does it provide?

  • Interactive Mars exploration: Lets users rotate, zoom, and inspect Mars on a 3D globe.
  • Scientific data in one place: Brings together imagery, elevation, thermal, geology, place-name, and rover map records.
  • Terrain-aware route exploration: Demonstrates how terrain and science context can inform route assessment beyond straight-line distance.
  • Historical mission context: Helps users explore recorded rover traverses, stops, and landing regions.
  • Educational accessibility: Makes planetary datasets and exploration-planning concepts easier to investigate through an interactive interface.

What is the intended impact?

AresNav aims to make Mars data more approachable and to encourage exploration of how scientific information can support planetary mission planning.

By connecting orbital map layers with route exploration, the project gives students, researchers, and space enthusiasts a way to investigate the Martian surface and consider factors that could affect travel. It also provides a starting point for future work on interactive planetary science and intelligent exploration planning.

AresNav is a research and demonstration prototype. Its routes and mission estimates are not operational guidance, and its results are not certified for mission use.

What technologies and resources did we use?

Development technologies:

  • JavaScript — frontend behavior, API logic, and terrain analysis.
  • Node.js — backend runtime and built-in test runner.
  • Express.js — API and web server.
  • CesiumJS — interactive 3D Mars globe.
  • HTML and CSS — application structure and styling.

Data resources:

  • NASA/JPL Mars Trek — Mars imagery, map features, place names, and rover records.
  • Viking MDIM 2.1 — global color mosaic.
  • MOLA/HRSC — elevation and terrain data used for map context and route sampling.
  • MGS TES — global thermal-inertia map layer.
  • USGS global geology — regional geological context.
  • Curiosity and Perseverance records — historical rover traverses, stops, and landing information.
  • Local demonstration data — example sites, hazards, routes, and environmental values.

Analysis techniques:

  • Slope, elevation variation, and roughness analysis.
  • Terrain traversal cost modeling.
  • Geological preferences and hazard buffers.
  • Crater-like depression screening from sampled elevation data.
  • Theta* pathfinding over a bounded terrain grid.

How is our project creative and innovative?

AresNav combines planetary visualization with an exploration-oriented route planner. Users can move from viewing Mars to inspecting its scientific layers and experimenting with how those layers might affect a route.

The route planner considers more than distance: it weighs sampled terrain, mapped geology, thermal-map transitions, and known hazards when searching for a lower-cost path. The app also places these features alongside historical rover records and provides a guided tour so users can discover the tools without needing prior experience with planetary mapping.

What factors did our team consider?

  1. Data sources and attribution: The app uses public NASA/JPL and USGS resources and links users to provider information.
  2. Data resolution: Orbital datasets vary in resolution and cannot reveal every small obstacle or surface condition.
  3. Uncertainty: Missing or unknown elevation samples are treated conservatively, and route results include confidence limitations.
  4. Performance: The terrain grid is bounded to control sampling and computation, which can make routes over large areas coarser.
  5. Historical versus live information: Rover paths are historical records, and mission telemetry values are demonstrations or estimates.
  6. Usability: A guided tour and interactive map controls help users explore the project’s features.
  7. Safety and scope: The route planner is experimental and does not replace validated mission systems or expert review.

Our Vision

Our vision is to make planetary exploration more interactive and understandable by connecting scientific data with practical exploration questions. AresNav is a step toward tools that help people investigate other worlds, understand the limits of available data, and explore how intelligent planning could support future missions.

Team: NeuroMars — Rohit Solanki and Gourav Jangid.
